name: The Courtier's Reply
statement: The courtier's reply dismisses a critic by claiming they lack the credentials or expertise to criticize, without addressing the substance.
statementAccent: claiming they lack the credentials or expertise to criticize
meaning: The courtier’s reply is an informal fallacy in which a response to criticism asserts that the critic hasn’t studied enough specialised literature or lacks proper qualifications, rather than showing how that overlooked expertise actually invalidates the criticism. It inverts appeal to authority: instead of citing an expert who supports a position, it gestures at unnamed expertise the critic supposedly lacks.
mechanism: The tactic shifts the burden onto the critic to first master an entire field before their objection can be considered, while never connecting that required expertise to a rebuttal of the specific point raised. This stalls debate and can shield claims from scrutiny indefinitely, since more "required reading" can always be invoked.

examples.text: PZ Myers coined the term in a December 2006 blog post responding to critics who argued Richard Dawkins could not criticise religion without first mastering theology, satirising it via a fable of the Emperor’s tailors and their treatises on invisible clothes.
Myers pointed to biologist H. Allen Orr’s critical review of "The God Delusion," which faulted Dawkins for not engaging sophisticated theology, as a real-world instance of the pattern.
Dawkins later made the same point, remarking that people happily reject fairies and astrology without first immersing themselves in the relevant "theological" literature.

whyItMatters: It helps distinguish legitimate expertise-based objections (which explain how the missing background changes the conclusion) from rhetorical stonewalling that never engages the claim: useful whenever a field’s insiders try to rule outsider criticism out of bounds by credentialism alone.
limits: Some genuine criticisms do require specialised background to evaluate, so invoking expertise is not always fallacious; critics of the concept, such as philosopher Edward Feser, argue it can itself be used to dodge substantive philosophical or theological objections.
misreadings: The fallacy applies specifically when credentials are invoked instead of substance; it is not committed simply by pointing out that a critic made a factual error within a specialised subject.
origin: American biologist PZ Myers coined "the courtier’s reply" in a Pharyngula blog post on 24 December 2006, framing it as a parody of "The Emperor’s New Clothes" in defence of Richard Dawkins.

sources.text: Courtier’s reply, Wikipedia. — PZ Myers’s December 2006 coinage and the Emperor’s New Clothes analogy.
PZ Myers, "The Courtier’s Reply," Pharyngula (24 December 2006), ScienceBlogs. — the original text of the parody.
